passages.text: And truly we tell you, on the day of judgment it will be more bearable to remain in the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than in the place of disobedience: first, because you did not recognize for yourselves what was reasonable; second, because, after hearing what concerned us, you did not come to us; third, because even when we came, you disobeyed us. Therefore, out of concern to spare you, we pray without charge that our peace may come upon you. So if you wish to possess this peace, you must eagerly undertake not to do wrong and nobly bear being wronged—something human nature could not endure unless it first received knowledge of what is beneficial above all, namely, knowledge of the righteous nature of the one who surpasses everything: that, in avenging those who are wronged, he exacts punishment and forever benefits those who act reverently.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνεκτότερον ἔσται γῇ Σοδόμων καὶ Γομόρρας ἐν ἡμέρᾳ κρίσεως ἢ τῷ τῆς ἀπειθείας τόπῳ ἐνδιατελεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: on the day of judgment it will be more bearable to remain in the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than in the place of disobedience
lexical_decisions.rationale: This takes the final infinitive ἐνδιατελεῖν as the subject of the impersonal comparison and both datives as parallel locations in which one remains. Alternatively, γῇ may depend directly on “more bearable” (“more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah”), while only the second dative goes with the infinitive, but that produces an uneven comparison.
The phrase denotes matters relating to the speakers without specifying whether these are their circumstances, message, or claims.
προῖκα conveys acting gratis or without payment. “Freely” is possible but could misleadingly suggest only willingness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μὴ ἀδικεῖν ἀναδέξασθαι καὶ τὸ ἀδικεῖσθαι γενναίως φέρειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: undertake not to do wrong and nobly bear being wronged
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two articular constructions contrast refraining from wrongdoing with enduring wrongdoing received from others.
The phrase describes the benefit as preeminent; “supremely advantageous” would be a more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in avenging those who are wronged, he exacts punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκδικῶν presents him as avenging the wronged, while τιμωρεῖ in this judicial context is rendered as imposing punishment. The latter verb can elsewhere carry the sense of aiding or avenging.
